Due to being 50 to 300 times the cost of an arc welder, the economics of an electron beam welding job shop are drastically different than an arc welding job shop. These very difficult financial headwinds incline electron beam welding job shops towards long term contracts and relationships, and away from short term high-engineering cost piecemeal work. A private non-OEM job shop needs to build a catalogue of qualified welds that have a good work flow (i.e high weld time to non-weld time). This ensures long-term relationships with government and private entities to manufacture and repair current products and develop new products for similar long-term manufacture and repair contracts. Proximity to relevant customers is beneficial to building these relationships. Due to the high capital cost of electron beam welding equipment and supporting facilities, job shops have their equipment running near capacity. Accommodating development or one-off jobs requires significant engineering investment without repeat of the same job and as such, there is little economic drive for a shop to prioritize this kind of high mix/low volume work compared to low mix/high volume work with clear revenue projection. Job shops also hesitate to take large contracts (e.g. 15days/month) that will result in neglecting or turning away work from their long-term customers. There is also a major concern related to past performance of requested jobs where the customers significantly overestimated their ability to produce parts for welding. Past customers have entered contracts with job shops then only met 50% of the promised production and eventually fell to 0%. These changes can be due to market conditions (down turn in aircraft engine demands) as well as governmental policy changes (reduction in defense spending). If the contract is large, this could mean serious financial problems for the jobs shop, and is a reason that it is preferred to spread the revenue generation across multiple projects and customers. In terms of spreading revenue generation, 6 days/month of welding is considered a large contract and an agreed upon contingency if the number of days was not met would be prudent. Furthermore, qualification may be needed on multiple machines in case issues were encountered. When approaching large contracts, it is suggested that a cost and materials first article development effort be completed before providing a detailed quote for series production. Sometimes the rough order of magnitude quotes can include a do not exceed clause, but the more mature the product and process is, the more accurate the quote can be. A job shop can operate on 1- or 2-part production with the caveat that the long-term customer and the job shop have a mutual understanding of the final product and timeline for production. These low and high production runs cannot sustain a business if the job shop is waiting for engineering decisions from customer; weld time is critical and if a machine is sitting idle, the shop is losing money.
